title: Error handling in class design
idea: Error handling decides which class detects a failure, what error type it throws, and which single layer catches it and turns it into a response.
points: Throw where you detect the problem; catch where you can act on it.
Custom error classes let callers branch with `instanceof`, not message text.
Wrap low-level errors with `{ cause }` so the original is kept.
Use `finally` for cleanup that must run on success or failure.

hero.title: A missing user travels back up

steps.caption: The request enters the controller, which calls the service.
The service asks the repository for user 7. It has no `try` block.
The database answers with no row.
The repository throws `NotFoundError`, a domain error, not a raw driver error.
The service cannot fix a missing user, so it lets the error pass up.
The controller catches it once, at the edge, and maps it to a `404` response.

code.title: An error hierarchy
code.caption: Error types carry the meaning; one table maps them to status codes. Add a `ConflictError` mapped to `409`.

walk.text: A base class sets `name` from the subclass, so logs show the real type.
Each failure kind is its own empty subclass; `AppError` already sets its `name`.
The finder throws at the point it detects the problem.
One place maps error types to HTTP status codes.
The edge matches with `instanceof`, so subclasses inherit a status; surprises fall back to `500`.

code.title: Wrap with a cause
code.caption: The low-level `SyntaxError` is wrapped in a domain error. `cause` keeps the original for logs and debugging.

pitfalls: Never leave a `catch` empty; it hides the failure and the bug.
Branch on error class or code, not on `e.message` text that may change.
Do not catch in every layer; catch only where you can recover or respond.

quiz.why: `finally` runs before `run` actually returns, so `cleanup` prints first. The caller then logs the returned `caught`.

takeaway: Throw typed errors where you detect them; catch once where you respond.
